persona: Global Basketball Apparel PLM Director - I run the SS28 global line across NA / GC / EMEA / APLA. I decide what earns a slot over what is already in the line, and I am accountable for line-plan productivity, franchise potential and full-price sell-through in four geographies, not for the elegance of an idea in one.
narrative:
I ranked on one question: does this deserve a slot over what already hangs in my line, in more than one geography, for more than one season? Three answers came back yes - not the three the priority spaces predict.

OPP-07 ranks first because it is the only candidate whose demand half is settled rather than argued. Women's basketball is the one signal the audit made STRONGER - three record seasons per game, a ratified CBA with the cap up roughly fivefold, growth achieved with Clark sidelined - and it is the only place Nike exclusively owns both halves of the outfit. The 61->41 cut is fair: the fixture the spec calls the whole opportunity is already built and already stocked with three Nike shorts, and USD 65-75 is argued off a fan wall discounting 25-45%. I fund the two free pulls that decide it, not the block.

OPP-03 ranks second on the strongest asymmetry here: highest adjusted confidence (48), the only reproducible consumer finding in 58 signals, and every decisive test uses data Nike already owns. The challenger is right that it is not a product opportunity - no silhouette, no length, no SKU, outside all three SS28 spaces. I carry that disagreement rather than resolve it: it consumes no line slot, so it does not compete with the other two - and no premium tier survives on a core that fails after one wash. Its business case is still wrong: USD 19 booked at retail markdown in a wholesale-weighted programme is partly a gift to Foot Locker.

OPP-02 ranks third on scalability, the criterion I use hardest. It is the only candidate multi-region and multi-season on day one, on the base's strongest cross-domain corroboration and an existing garment. I buy the naming, laddering and rack-legibility programme; not the wet-and-stretched UPF certification, which existing standards already cover and any competitor can elect in one cycle.

Below the line: OPP-08 carries the most damning verified observation - Nike's Big & Tall basketball offer is its two cheapest franchises - but that inversion is confounded with franchise tiering and the UK ladder does not reproduce it; EXPLORE, via the near-free test of an 11" in premium DNA. OPP-06 splits: Doha sits inside confirmed FIBA rights, LA28 belongs to Fanatics, Ralph Lauren and FOURTEEN, so kill it today. OPP-05 earns EXPLORE for its research gate only - Europe is the primary market of under 2% of this base - but EmpCo is a prohibition regime where silence is free, so its moat inverts and its garment duplicates OPP-02 and OPP-03. OPP-04 is WATCH: its proving-ground mechanism is arithmetically void, so instrument the Australian doors under OPP-02. OPP-01 is the only REJECT: Nike already sells that bottoms system through the dealer it names.

Note: five of eight were talked down because nobody audited Nike's live line, and three free internal pulls - unit share by inseam, realised ASP and markdown by door, returns by defect code - would move four of these scores.
weighting_rationale: I weighted to the job, not to the excitement. COMMERCIAL POTENTIAL (16) and CONSUMER NEED (13) and EVIDENCE STRENGTH (13) carry the most, because a line slot is a bet with a booked cost and this base has a specific pathology the audit named: no first-party Nike commercial data anywhere, not one price confirmed against a retrieved page, three mutually incompatible Nike price ladders coexisting, and report-mill numbers counted as convergence. In that condition, evidence quality is not a tiebreaker - it is a gate, so I score it as heavily as need. SCALABILITY (11) is next and is the criterion I use most aggressively, because I am allergic to ideas that only work in one market or one season; a franchise that lives in one country is a country manager's project, not a global line item, and I have marked OPP-04 down to a 1 and OPP-08 down to a 2 on exactly that basis even though both carry good structural evidence. PRODUCT DIFFERENTIATION (12) is high because the single systemic failure across all seven specialists - flagged identically by all seven skeptics - was proposing product Nike already ships; differentiation here is scored as 'newness against Nike's own live line', which is why OPP-02, OPP-03 and OPP-05 all score 1-2 despite otherwise strong cases. NIKE RIGHT TO WIN (10) matters because half this portfolio's moats inverted under challenge - team colour at scale, wet-state UPF certification, EmpCo asymmetry - each collapsing when the challenger showed the capability was either already deployed or purchasable by a competitor in one cycle. MARKET WHITESPACE (8) is deliberately DOWN-weighted: PAT-02 shows three domains independently declared outdoor function, storage and UPF unowned, and one live SKU (FN2659) closed all three - that is one un-run catalogue query counted three times. Whitespace claims in this base are mostly search artifacts, so I refuse to let them carry weight. BASKETBALL AUTHENTICITY (7) is meaningful but modest: it is a licence to operate, not a differentiator, since every candidate here is a basketball short. CULTURAL RELEVANCE (5) is low on purpose - the culture evidence is the weakest layer in the base (Pinterest percentages with no absolute base, F1 and Brazil terms growing as fast as the basketball ones, Accio-laundered retro data the audit struck) and the audit rated retro/swingman durability 'unclear'. RISK (5) is low-weighted not because risk is unimportant but because it is already priced into the other nine and into the challengers' adjusted confidence; double-counting it would punish the honest specs twice - and the honest specs (OPP-01, OPP-02, OPP-03) are the ones that disclosed their own defects before the red team found them. Overall = sum(score x weight) / 5, giving a 20-100 range. Categories are NOT a pure function of the composite: category answers 'what does the next dollar buy'. That is why OPP-05 at 45.8 is EXPLORE (its ask IS a cheap research gate that closes the portfolio's biggest structural hole) while OPP-04 at 46.8 is WATCH (its ask is an early line commit whose stated justification is arithmetically void).

scores.rationale: The only opportunity the red-team declared dead (survives=false, 52 -> 26), and I agree with the verdict for a reason that is specifically a PLM reason: the challenger opened the order form this programme proposes to build and found the product already on it. Nike Team Sports already structures basketball Bottoms as Shorts / Pants / Tights & Capris; BSN - the named lead dealer - already lists the Nike Pro 3/4 Length Tight as a team SKU in Team Navy, Team Royal and Team Maroon; and Nike Team Sports already publishes a cross-style stock colour chart. That single check collapses the novelty claim, the 'colour at scale' moat and the soft-micro-dealer competitive read at once. Worse, there is a rules error inside the spec: A06-S3 records that NFHS keys tights to the JERSEY colour (white, black, beige or predominant jersey colour) while Rule 3-4-5 governs bottoms-to-bottoms, so the headline dE<=1.0 short-to-tight tolerance - which the spec calls 'the entire product' - is engineered against a pair no cited rule regulates, and for most rosters the compliant tight is black and already sells at USD 37. The price argument also inverts: Nike's own stock Pro 3/4 street-prices USD 26.97-32.00, below the proposed USD 30-36 team NET, and a no-minimum custom supplier exists at USD 47.88, so neither the price nor the minimum-order switching case survives. On timing, the dev agent honestly broke its own why-now (Rule 3-4-5 is 2023-24, not 2025-26); the challenger then showed the NSGA briefed dealers on it in 2023, so three ordering cycles of silence is a market verdict as easily as a whitespace. What I will NOT throw away: the enabling rule is primary, dated and independently re-verified, and one silhouette in the family - a loose full-length game PANT on the short's block - could not be found as stock product from any brand. That is a team-catalogue merchant's ticket (one pant SKU, a knee-clearing size-grade certification, a printed 20-wash spec on the dealer sheet), not an SS28 line slot. Scored low on scalability because the entire architecture rests on one governing body: FIBA's multiple-styles position is unconfirmed, assets.fiba.basketball was egress-blocked, and France's hijab ban removes the modest-dress leg in a core European market. Basketball authenticity is the one strong score - a rulebook-driven competition garment is as authentic as this category gets.
scores.biggest_risk: Building a 12-colour x 4-bottom x full-size-grade x two-block CARRYOVER stock library against a need nobody has counted. The addressable base is the roster (896,944 US high-school participants), but the addressable NEED is the unmeasured subset wanting a non-standard bottom - and the compliant tight for most of those teams is black, which Nike already stocks. Carryover inventory risk with no demand denominator, on a channel signal (A04-S9) that contains no basketball-shorts data of any kind and whose revenue base the auditor contradicted.

scores.rationale: The most globally scalable idea in the portfolio and the only one whose garment already exists in the doors it needs to win - which is exactly why I fund the merchandising and franchise move and refuse the certification programme. The consumer need is the strongest cross-domain corroboration in the base (PAT-11): peer-reviewed physiology (A06-S2, 0.00-1.33 kg of trapped sweat, VERIFIED), documented institutional behaviour change in the Philippines and India (A06-S5, meets moved off the 9am-3pm window from 2024), and a competitor's multi-season commercial platform in Li-Ning Wade UPF 50+ (A03-S7) - three pools sharing no source. The S.T. Flare precedent (A01-S7, VERIFIED) is a genuinely unique Nike asset: Nike has already made and marketed this consumer argument one category over. The channel read is VERIFIED (A02-S7, A04-S1). But the challenger took 62 -> 40 on three live retrievals I have to respect. First, the white space was a search artifact - FN2659 already ships UVA/UVB, side pockets, a phone-secure zip pocket and a rebound-durability claim, merchandised on Nike AU/IN/MY/ID/JP and at Rebel. Second, the differentiator is not a first: AATCC 183 already provides a wet test state and ASTM D6603 already conditions and documents the stretch effect, so 'UPF certified wet and stretched' is a purchasable test election Li-Ning can answer in one cycle - and ARPANSA certifies per material AND per colour, which makes the certified-block strategy and the city-graphic capsule strategy economically incompatible. Third, the price is contradicted by the shelves the spec names: DNA 8" at 50% off, DNA 6" realised at USD 37.50, UV Woven at AUD 44.99 against an AUD 75-80 ask - and NORTHYARD already ships UPF 50+ at 5/7/9 inseams, unlined, zip-pocketed and reflective, with 'basketball' in the title, in Amazon's best-seller ranks. So I score differentiation at 2 and whitespace at 2 and still invest, because what remains is the highest-productivity move available to a line planner: name a franchise, ladder it from one inseam to 5/7/9, extend the women's block, put a legible spec block on a rack that carries no product copy, and take it into GC, APLA, the Gulf, the Sun Belt and Australia off live inventory. Scalability 5 is the reason it is top three; it is the only candidate that is genuinely multi-region and multi-season on day one. HYPOTHESIS, not finding: that findability, not function, is the binding constraint - nobody has measured it.
scores.biggest_risk: That the whole prize is a USD 5 list-price step on a SKU realising USD 37.50, and even that does not hold. The certification premium is answerable by any competitor, Nike's own standing claims policy defines Dri-FIT UV as 'minimum UPF 30' and declines to print a UPF number even in Australia (reversing that is a legal and brand-governance programme across the whole platform, not a hangtag change), and the total sun-protective apparel category is roughly USD 1.4B by 2030 across every garment and sport. Second-order: the UPF story is hung on the thigh - the one region a basketball short already covers - while A06-S5 documents heat pushing play to dawn and dusk in the priority markets.

scores.rationale: Highest adjusted confidence in the portfolio (60 -> 48) and the highest-certainty dollar in it, and I am funding it with my eyes open to the challenger's tenth kill attempt - that this is not a product opportunity at all. That attack is correct on its own terms: it changes no silhouette, adds no length, adds no SKU, opens no market, sits outside all three SS28 priority spaces, and would be executed by Materials, Sourcing and Quality rather than by PLM. My answer is that it therefore does not compete for a line slot, and line-plan productivity is my job before newness is. The consumer defect is the only reproducible consumer finding in 58 signals and it got STRONGER under attack: the challenger tried to dismiss it as a review-venue artifact and instead reproduced 'falling apart after a few wears' on a DIFFERENT SKU (Icon 11") at a THIRD retailer, on top of Icon+ 6" at 3.9 stars / 67% recommend across 64 reviews at Dick's (A04-S6) and the Walmart corpus (A01-S3). Stated WTP for durable construction in activewear is 43% and rising. The financial frame is an audited filing (A03-S9: FY26 apparel +2% cn, units +1%, ASP from mix and already eroded by discounts) and the channel read is VERIFIED (A02-S7). Above all, every decisive test is data Nike already owns - warranty defect codes, BOM/GSM history, markdown allowances by partner - obtainable in weeks for tens of thousands of dollars, with an explicit stop-gate ('no drift, no failure, stop the programme'). That asymmetry is why it ranks second. What comes off, following the challenger: the USD 19/unit recovery is booked at RETAIL markdown in a programme weighted 70/30 to WHOLESALE, so Nike recovers it only through negotiated markdown allowances at a rate nobody has quoted while carrying 100% of the BOM increment; the '20W' badge anchors below the 100+ washes contract sourcing treats as normal for team mesh and fails its own season-of-weekly-washing job story; Nike already claims 'lightweight-yet-durable' and 'built for the grind' on DNA, so this substantiates an existing claim rather than opening a new one; Decathlon already guarantees two years and publishes calculated lifespans from below; and EmpCo plus France's October 2026 environmental-cost display with a 0.67-1.45 durability coefficient make durability a mandated comparative metric, not a free claim. Differentiation 2 and whitespace 2 reflect all of that honestly. Carried forward unresolved: nobody has established that GSM ever changed. The premise may be false - and settling it is the first deliverable, not the last.
scores.biggest_risk: That Legal will not let us print a number, and that the number we could print is one we cannot afford. A specific numeric longevity claim converts marketing puffery into an implied warranty across tens of millions of units in the same season EmpCo makes unsubstantiated DURABILITY claims specifically sanctionable; the 20-cycle AATCC 135 gate is roughly 7x the standard three-cycle run, per colourway, per lot, across contract factories Nike does not own, in a year of USD 1.5B annualised tariff cost and 120bp of gross-margin headwind; and every scaled make-guarantee precedent (L.L.Bean 15% abuse / ~USD 250M, REI, Dr Martens) was retracted. Applied uniformly to Icon and DNA it also flattens the ladder it was designed to defend.

scores.rationale: This is the opportunity my role is built to say no to, and it hurts, because the market read is the best-verified non-US evidence in the entire base and every skeptic correction ran in its favour (A02-S9; A05-S6 verifies verbatim against the NBL's own 1,231,796 / +9% / 63 sell-outs release; NBL27 dates confirm exactly). The challenger still took it 61 -> 38, and the decisive break is arithmetic, not opinion: the ENTIRE case is that an Australia-first drop returns a season of sell-through BEFORE the SS28 global buy commits, and on Nike's futures calendar the SS28 buy closes around the month the Australian range would land, with line-lock a year before that. The read can only steer SS29, and the Australian product must itself be committed before it proves anything. Remove the proving-ground mechanism and the spec's own sentence applies - evidence quality alone is not a reason to spend. Everything else compounds: the dual-state UPF differentiator is already occupied (AS/NZS 4399 contemplates wet/stretched as an optional protocol, and Sheila and Sun2Sea already market 'wet or dry' to Australians), Cancer Council Australia sells UPF50+ shorts itself and recommends long pants, the +25% female figure straddles a documented AusPlay instrument break (phone to online panel, July 2023, ASC says the series restarts), Australia has roughly 800 courts against China's 1.1M+ and its basketball is organised around indoor club stadiums, AUD 79.99 sits above every observable point on the Australian shelf (UV Woven AUD 69.99 is the ceiling; Champion's NBL wall tops at AUD 61.95; an independent search returns DNA 6" at AUD 44.99), and Nike holds no Australian basketball rights at all - iAthletic supplies the Boomers and Opals, Champion holds the NBL, Foot Locker sponsors the Boomers. APLA apparel is USD 1,629M flat across ~40 countries; Australian Nike basketball shorts is plausibly a low-single-digit-million-dollar class, which is not enough denominator for a read by inseam x gender x price x door. Scalability 1 is not a slight on Australia; it is the finding that trade press states directly ('Australia is no test market'). WATCH rather than REJECT because the residue is real and free: Nike already sells a 6/8/10/11" DNA ladder and the UV Woven through Rebel, JD and Foot Locker AU, so pull eight quarters of that sell-through THIS quarter under OPP-02 and instrument Australia as a lead door in the global franchise rather than as a separate programme.
scores.biggest_risk: Committing a range six to nine months early at a price no Australian has paid, to buy a dataset we can get for free this quarter from product already on the Rebel shelf - and then discovering the read does not generalise anyway. Australia's UPF literacy, price level, retail structure, indoor club orientation and inverted season are all distinctive, so a clean Australian sell-through would say very little about Greater China, SEA, the Gulf or the US Sun Belt, which is where the OPP-02 volume actually is.

scores.rationale: Lowest adjusted confidence in the portfolio (34 -> 24) and I am still categorising it EXPLORE, because category here answers 'what does the next dollar buy', not 'what is the composite'. What this opportunity actually asks for is a minimum viable European read - and the cross-dataset audit independently instructed the same thing before ranking. As the person who runs NA / GC / EMEA / APLA, the single most alarming line in the audit is that Europe, Nike's second geography, is the primary market of essentially zero signals (under 2% of the base) and enters the analysis only as a compliance deadline, a markdown line, a set of doors and a Li-Ning clearance price. Meanwhile EuroLeague set a fourth consecutive attendance record at 3,251,706 (+8%) and the DBB hit an all-time-high 288,444 memberships (+5.26%), and none of it is in any specialist file. I am funding the read. I am rejecting the garment as specified, for the three reasons the challenger found. (1) The moat inverts: the EU withdrew the Green Claims Directive (June 2025) - the substantiation instrument - and kept EmpCo, a prohibition instrument, under which silence is compliant and free. Every competitor complies by deleting one line of hangtag copy. That is a floor, not a moat. (2) Portfolio duplication: the published 20-wash ISO 6330 spec is OPP-03's central proposition and the certified UPF claim is OPP-02's, both at higher confidence and both already naming UK/Germany/France. Continental's undisclosed incremental content is a name, a palette and a jacquard waistband - hence differentiation 1. (3) The founding 'European void' claim is overstated in its own base (two Trustpilot observations exist, one geo-tagged United Kingdom, both negative), and the price anchor may be inverted - if Nike's live European price is EUR 52-58, EUR 45 de-rates existing business rather than creating a rung. Add the contradictions the developer disclosed honestly: the only European growth number in the base (Grand View 4.9% CAGR) makes Europe the SLOWEST region named, the only registry-grade European youth number is Sport England's SIGNIFICANT 1% DECREASE in weekly under-16 players, and EMEA is precisely where Nike's promotional damage is measured (-6% revenue, Digital -24%). Evidence strength 1 is the honest score for a proposition its own author called unfalsifiable. Note the internal inconsistency the challenger caught: the largest European participation number in the base is English, and the spec puts the UK in Tier 3.
scores.biggest_risk: That we mistake an evidence vacuum for a market opening and fund a Europe-created franchise, a 27-jurisdiction claims architecture and a governed EUR 35 markdown floor in the one region where Nike's own results show it cannot hold price - and where it has never demonstrated basketball-apparel creation authority. The cheap failure mode is worse than the expensive one: the single un-run query is Nike's own live EMEA basketball assortment, SKU count, inseam mix and price ladder. Three of seven specialists were already burned proposing product Nike ships.

scores.rationale: Explore the DOHA half; kill the VALLEY half now, before anyone builds a deck around a home Games we do not own. The challenger resolved this opportunity's own top unknown IN ITS FAVOUR - Nike is FIBA's official product partner across apparel, footwear and equipment for flagship national-team competitions with the 2027 World Cup named explicitly - so a Doha-anchored capsule sits inside existing rights on an existing chassis, which is a real and cheap thing. Everything else went the other way, 57 -> 39. The mechanism has a Nike-specific disconfirmation the spec never looked for: Nike guided the Paris 2024 Olympic quarter down about 10%, its first Olympic-quarter decline since at least Sydney 2000, with product in 8,000+ doors - which converts 'a dated moment pulls full price' from a proven mechanism into a rights-and-marketing-dependent one (adidas' +35% came with EUR 212M of incremental World Cup marketing and the kit rights to the teams people were watching). The same FIBA agreement runs 2017-2027 with no renewal found, so the 'chassis survives to 2031' argument fails and the sequencing inverts: Doha is a closing window, not a pilot. At LA28, Fanatics holds merchandise, licensing and venue retail, Ralph Lauren is Official Outfitter, FIBA 3x3 apparel belongs to FOURTEEN from 2026, and Mitchell & Ness already has LA28-marked swingman shorts at retail two years early - so the VALLEY leg, the 3x3 hero framing and ~20% of the proposed channel mix are all rights Nike does not hold. The product content is thinner than claimed (Aero-FIT shipped on a basketball short 17 July 2026 at USD 75; FN2659 already carries UPF plus a phone-sized zip pocket), the price anchor is discounting in its own moment year (USMNT replica short USD 55 -> USD 44 with code), and Jordan already runs an annual dated, place-anchored streetball capsule with shorts in it at Quai 54. Scale check: the 2023 FIBA World Cup drew 700,665 spectators total, about 64% of one NBL season; Qatar's entire sports market across all sports is ~USD 955M. And the consumer behaviour is inferred, never observed - the strongest fan-fashion term in the base is a JERSEY term (+494%), which argues for tops. Cultural relevance 4 and basketball authenticity 4 are genuine and are why this is not a REJECT. Scalability 2 because a non-replenishable dated capsule is the structural opposite of franchise potential - and strip the date and the three styles are OPP-01, OPP-02 and OPP-07/08, competing with them for the same buy.
scores.biggest_risk: Building a two-drop chassis on rights that lapse between the drops. Doha 2027 is covered; LA28 is not, and the gate the programme calls its best feature may not even close in time - a week-8 read on a Jul-Sep 2027 Doha drop arrives Oct-Nov 2027, roughly when the SS28 wholesale books have to be written. Secondary and nearly as bad: wholesale partners buy replenishable core, and there is no evidence anywhere in this base that anyone buys a basketball SHORT at a national-team moment.

scores.rationale: Ranks first because it is the only place in this portfolio where the demand half is settled rather than argued, and where Nike's right to win is exclusive rather than merely strong. Women's basketball demand is the one signal the audit made STRONGER: three consecutive record seasons on a per-game basis, a 2026 All-Star crowd of 19,783 that outdrew the NBA's for the first time, 73 million unique viewers at the halfway mark, a ratified seven-year CBA with the team cap up roughly fivefold - and the single-athlete concentration risk stress-tested in the field, because the league grew with Caitlin Clark sidelined for much of 2026. Four independent instruments agree on the shape (A05-S7 VERIFIED event economics, A04-S5 a first-party retailer call-out, A02-S9 registry participation in a second country, A01-S1 a large teen panel). Nike designs the WNBA on-court uniform including the 2026 Rebel Edition programme, holds Sabrina and A'ja Wilson and adds Caitlin Clark from 1 October 2026, and put Aero-FIT onto a women's signature short FIRST. If the job is literally 'the other half of a Nike jersey', only Nike controls the trim, placket, colour standard and drop calendar on both halves - Mitchell & Ness owns the retro fan bottom at USD 80 with no on-court top to match, and Fanatics distributes but does not design the block. That is a 5 on right to win and a 5 on authenticity, and it is squarely in the SS28 Women's Revolution space. Now the 20 points the challenger took off, which I have honoured. The opportunity's OWN stated kill condition - 'if the fixture change cannot be secured, do not make the product, because the fixture IS the opportunity' - is met in the wrong direction: the fixture already exists, is already occupied, and is occupied by Nike. Fanatics runs a Ladies WNBA Shorts category stocked with Nike Legends Flow Mesh at USD 74.99, On-Court Victory at USD 84.99 and Logowoman Crossover at USD 49.99; Nike's own WNBA pages carry Victory knee-length at USD 85 and Crossover WNBA at USD 60; Rebel Fanwear shorts have been in fan doors since 8 May 2026; the Clark collection already pairs a logo tee with a logo short. Hence whitespace 2. The USD 65-75 rung is argued from a fan wall discounting 25-45% with codes, against a Sabrina realising USD 42.97. And the attribution is pan-sport, not basketball: 'F1 aesthetic outfit' +483% and 'Brazil jersey outfit women' +302% grow as fast, which the auditor instructed be discarded as basketball evidence. So what I am funding is NOT the block - it is the two first-party pulls that decide it, both free: what did the Rebel Fanwear short and the Clark short actually sell, and what share of women's basketball fan units are bottoms rather than tops. Preserve the open disagreement: Ed Stack described 'boys and girls, young men and women' buying this product, which argues a unisex fan block in a women's size run rather than a women's-graded block - a real fork this analysis has not resolved.
scores.biggest_risk: That the answer is merchandising and pricing, and Nike has already given it. A fourth Nike women's short into a fixture already clearing three of them at a third off adds ASP nowhere and splits demand three ways against the Clark, Sabrina and Rebel Edition programmes already funded - in a +1% unit environment. Underneath that sits the cohort risk: Piper Sandler showed a 13-point drop in Nike mindshare among female teens with female share under 40% for the first time since 2020, and Nike's teen APPAREL mindshare is 26%, not the widely-quoted 49% footwear figure. We would be trying to win a fan-fashion occasion with the one consumer where our measured standing is falling.

scores.rationale: Second-highest adjusted confidence (58 -> 44) and it contains the single most damning verified observation in the portfolio: Nike's Big & Tall basketball assortment at Kohl's is composed of exactly its two CHEAPEST franchises, DNA Academy 11" and Icon 11" - one of which carries the seam-failure review corpus from A04-S6. Nike offers no premium-make basketball short in extended sizes in the biggest big-and-tall door. That is a real architecture defect, it is entirely Nike's to fix unilaterally with no competitor set needing to move, and AND1 at USD 9.98 to 5XL and Mitchell & Ness on licensed IP cannot follow up-market. Right to win 4. But four challenger attacks landed and none is resolvable from public data, so this is EXPLORE, not INVEST. (1) The headline inversion is confounded: Nike UK - a market the brief never checked - shows the franchise premium at constant length is GBP 20 while the length effect at constant franchise is GBP 12, so the finding is roughly a third the size claimed and is substantially 'Nike's entry line is cheap'. (2) The rung already exists inside the premium franchise: DNA 8" at USD 55 and DNA 10" at USD 50, which fails the NEW test this engine is supposed to enforce - hence differentiation 2. (3) The trade-up is nearly double, not half again: Kohl's is selling the Big & Tall DNA Academy 11" at USD 27.75, not USD 37, against a USD 55 ask, with no willingness-to-pay evidence anywhere. (4) The load-bearing decision - full size run, both lengths, six colours, price parity, held in physical doors - is exactly Old Navy BODEQUALITY, retrenched within nine months for over-planned large sizes and excess inventory, and extended sizes carry 3-5 points lower gross margin on fabric consumption alone before any GSM increase. Add: the coverage-first need is a HYPOTHESIS on 2014-2017 sources (the Griner quote is May 2014, the Minnesota work 2015-2017) and Nike has run a modest collection since 2017 without ever adding a long women's basketball bottom - nine years of revealed preference; the AND1 buyer may be a price buyer, evidenced by one anonymous review; and the waist-control thesis rests on Nike's generic women's-bottoms sizing boilerplate (A06-S9), which is standard industry practice, not a basketball finding. Scalability 2 is the score that keeps this out of my top three: the UK ladder does not reproduce the US shape, so the inversion may be a US price-file artifact rather than a global architecture problem, and I will not fund an architecture on one market's price file. Carried forward unresolved and NOT averaged: A07-S4 argues the poles, A02-S5's own cited source says 7-9", and Nike's live ladder runs 6-11" continuously. Unit share by inseam appears nowhere in seven specialist files, three skeptic rounds or the audit - and it is the number this decision turns on.
scores.biggest_risk: That the whole thing is a price-file memo and the cheapest kill test defeats the programme: list an 11" inside the premium DNA franchise at USD 50-55 for one season in existing fabric, and if it works, no SS28 architecture, no heavier GSM and no same-price 4XL commitment was ever needed. If it does not work, we learn the coverage buyer is a price buyer. Either way the risk is cannibalisation on the same rail - a USD 55 Full Range 11" hanging beside a USD 27.75 Academy 11" in the same door, same silhouette, same palette, deliberately without graphics to separate them, most likely producing a split buy rather than a trade-up.
